text.p: The backdown by the government on means testing, announced yesterday by Education Minister Amanda Vanstone, came as a result of backbench pressure.
This development suggests some hope of a sensible budget outcome on May 13.
John Howard has a large backbench, many of them politically naive, believing they have been sent to Canberra to do something and are prepared to make a noise in the party room.
This is not how the Coalition party room traditionally behaves.

With parliament's resumption this week these backbenchers are aware of the clear signs of the economy picking up -- the Reserve Bank has signalled no more interest cuts; skilled vacancy jobs are on the rise; imports on the increase; and company profits have shot to a record high in the three months to December.
In short the outlook is much better than a mere three weeks ago when Treasurer Peter Costello unveiled the mid-year review showing a budget deficit blowout of A$2.9 billion.
What backbenchers and business will be urging is for the Howard government to adopt a budget strategy which is not ideologically driven by Treasury to get the deficit under control at all costs.

Backbenchers and business will be urging that, with no real risk of a reignition of inflation, the budget should have as its number one priority encouraging the lift in the economy, rather than risk strangling it.
Certainly the argument against further cuts in business support programmes has strengthened immeasurably in the last three weeks.
Meanwhile, there has been a change in plan on the release of the Mortimer review of government business programmes.
There was to be an interim report in time for consideration as part of the budget.
But this has not turned out to be practical and the Mortimer report will not come before the Cabinet until after the budget.
John Moore now has a very strong argument that there certainly should be no further cuts to business programmes in the budget until the Mortimer review has been dealt with in mid-year.
